# Outside Time Limits for a De Novo Request Accepted Without an Additional-Information Submission — 21 CFR Part 860 as in Force on 2026-11-21

**Status of this document.** Draft prepared for review by a qualified clinician/regulatory professional. It is not legal advice and is not for patient care. Every regulatory statement below is tied to a quoted source listed in Section 8.

---

## 1. Question as answered

FDA receives a De Novo request under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 360c(f)(2)). FDA accepts the request for substantive review **without** issuing a refusal-to-accept and **without** the requester later submitting additional information that results in acceptance. Asked: (a) the outside time limit for FDA's acceptance notification; (b) the outside time limit for FDA's review and its order granting or declining the request.

**Scope assumptions applied (they define the scenario, they are not findings):** only the formal regulatory outside limits in 21 CFR Part 860 are in scope, not MDUFA user-fee performance goals; "accepted without any additional-information submission" means acceptance on the first pass, with no additional-information submission of the kind described in § 860.230(c)(3); 2026-11-21 is the date on which the regulatory framework is assessed, not a submission date.

---

## 2. Answer

| # | Item | Outside limit | Clock starts | Governing citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | FDA notification of whether the De Novo request is accepted | **15 days** | Date FDA receives the De Novo request | 21 CFR 860.230(a) |
| (b) | FDA review completed and order granting or declining the request sent to the requester | **120 days** | Date FDA receives the De Novo request (the additional-information restart in § 860.230(c)(3) does not apply in this scenario) | 21 CFR 860.240(a) |

**Units and counting convention.** Both limits are expressed in **calendar days**. The regulation states "days" without qualification. Counting convention used throughout this memo: the day FDA receives the request is **day 0**, and the due date is the receipt date **plus** the stated number of calendar days. This convention follows § 860.230(b), which fixes "the date of acceptance" as "the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA" — i.e., the anchor is the receipt date, not the date the acceptance notice issues.

**Derived figure (arithmetic, not a regulatory limit).** If the acceptance notification issues on the last permissible day (day 15), the remaining substantive-review period before the day-120 order deadline is 120 − 15 = **105 calendar days**. This figure is below the 120-day bound and is offered only to show how the two clocks nest.

**Key structural point.** In this scenario the two clocks run from the **same** start date. A late acceptance notice does not push the 120-day order deadline, because § 860.230(b) deems the request accepted if FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, and § 860.240(a) measures the 120 days from receipt of the request.

---

## 3. Governing text, quoted

### 3.1 Acceptance notification — 21 CFR 860.230(a)

> "The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. **Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.**"

Note the object of the 15-day obligation: FDA must notify the requester **whether** the request has been accepted — the limit covers the yes/no determination, not merely the issuance of an acceptance letter.

### 3.2 Deemed acceptance and the anchor date — 21 CFR 860.230(b)

> "If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. **The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.**"

Consequence: a request accepted by operation of the regulation (FDA missing the 15-day window) is still anchored to the original receipt date for the 120-day clock.

### 3.3 The restart provision that does **not** apply here — 21 CFR 860.230(c)(3)

> "If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. The additional information must include the De Novo request reference number of the original submission. **If the De Novo request is subsequently accepted, the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information.**"

This is the only mechanism in the quoted text that re-anchors the acceptance date. Because the stated scenario is acceptance without any additional-information submission, no re-anchoring occurs and the 120 days run from receipt of the original request.

### 3.4 Review and order — 21 CFR 860.240(a)

> "FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. **Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b).**"

The obligation is to **send the requester an order** within 120 days. It is discharged by either an order granting (§ 860.260(a)) or an order declining (§ 860.260(b)) — the 120-day limit is a deadline for a decision of either kind, not a guarantee of a grant.

### 3.5 Order types — 21 CFR 860.260(a)(1)–(2) (context)

> "(a)(1) FDA will issue to the requester an order granting a De Novo request if none of the reasons in paragraph (c) of this section for declining the De Novo request applies. (2) If FDA grants a De Novo request, **within 30 days after the issuance of an order granting the De Novo request**, FDA will publish in the Federal Register a notice of the classification order, including any special controls."

The 30-day Federal Register publication step is a separate, downstream obligation and is **not** part of the 120-day review-and-order limit.

---

## 4. Version of Part 860 in force on 2026-11-21

**Determination.** The text in force on 2026-11-21 is the eCFR "current" text of 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D, which incorporates the amendment published at **90 FR 55980 (Dec. 4, 2025)**. The source note of § 860.240 reads: "[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]".

**What that amendment changed, and what it did not.** Comparing the two texts side by side:

| Provision | govinfo, CFR 2025 annual edition (edition date 2025-04-01) | eCFR current (fetched 2026-11-23) |
|---|---|---|
| § 860.230(a) | "Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted." | Identical |
| § 860.240(a) | "Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting ... or an order declining ..." | Identical |
| § 860.240(c)(2) | "... implementation of **Quality System Regulation** (part 820 of this chapter) requirements ..." | "... implementation of **Quality Management System Regulation (part 820 of this chapter)** requirements ..." |

The December 4, 2025 amendment is a conforming nomenclature edit in § 860.240(c)(2) implementing the Quality Management System Regulation. **It does not touch either time limit.** Accordingly the answer — 15 days and 120 days — is identical under both the pre-amendment and post-amendment texts, and is insensitive to which of the two governs on 2026-11-21.

---

## 5. Clock mechanics in the stated scenario

1. **Day 0** — FDA receives the De Novo request. This single date anchors both clocks (§ 860.230(b) last sentence; § 860.240(a)).
2. **Day 15** — outside limit for FDA to notify the requester whether the request is accepted (§ 860.230(a)). If FDA does not complete the acceptance review by then, the request is accepted by operation of § 860.230(b) and FDA must still notify.
3. **Days 15–120** — substantive review. FDA may require additional information during review (§ 860.240(b)(1)) and the requester may supplement or amend the pending request (§ 860.240(b)).
4. **Day 120** — outside limit for FDA to send an order granting (§ 860.260(a)) or declining (§ 860.260(b)) (§ 860.240(a)).
5. **Day 120 + 30** — if the order grants the request, outside limit for Federal Register publication of the classification order notice (§ 860.260(a)(2)). Separate obligation, outside the scope of the two limits asked about.

**Does additional information during substantive review toll the 120-day clock?** On the quoted text, no tolling provision exists: § 860.240(a) provides a single re-anchoring trigger — "receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230" — which is the § 860.230(c)(3) post-refusal cure, expressly excluded by the stated scenario. § 860.240(b) permits additional information to be required or submitted but attaches no clock effect. This is a reading of the fetched text, flagged for confirmation at V-3.

**MDUFA performance goals are not cited as the answer.** FDA's user-fee (MDUFA) performance goals for De Novo review operate on a different basis (including goal dates and clock-stop conventions) and are not the regulatory outside limits in Part 860. They are named here only so that a reader does not conflate the two numbers.

---

## 6. Worked example (hypothetical dates, illustrative only)

Hypothetical receipt date: **2027-01-04** (day 0).

| Milestone | Computation | Date | Within limit? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acceptance notification due | 2027-01-04 + 15 calendar days | **2027-01-19** (day 15) | Yes — exactly at the § 860.230(a) limit |
| Order granting or declining due | 2027-01-04 + 120 calendar days: 27 days to Jan 31 (day 27); +28 days to Feb 28 (day 55); +31 days to Mar 31 (day 86); +30 days to Apr 30 (day 116); +4 days to May 4 (day 120) | **2027-05-04** (day 120) | Yes — exactly at the § 860.240(a) limit |

2027 is not a leap year, so February has 28 days in this computation. Under the alternative convention (receipt day counted as day 1) each date would fall one day earlier; the convention used is stated in Section 2 so the arithmetic is reproducible.

---

## 7. Adjacent deadlines deliberately excluded from the answer

These are named so the reader can see they were considered and are **not** the 15-day or 120-day limits:

- **180 days** — the requester's window to provide a complete response to deficiencies identified under § 860.230(c)(2) before FDA may consider the request withdrawn (grounds listed at § 860.250(a)(2), as quoted in the fetched Part 860 page). Applies only after a refusal to accept.
- **30 days** — Federal Register publication of a classification order after a granting order (§ 860.260(a)(2)).
- **No stated limit** — the timing of a facility inspection that FDA may conduct prior to granting or declining (§ 860.240(c)); the regulation authorizes the inspection but sets no deadline for it.
- **MDUFA performance goals** — out of scope (Section 5).

---

## 8. Source register

| ID | Source | Full citation | Locator as fetched | Fetched (UTC) | SHA-256 (prefix) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | eCFR, § 860.230 | 21 CFR 860.230, "Accepting a De Novo request" (current as of fetch; incorporates amendments through 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025) | https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-860/subpart-D/section-860.230 | 2026-11-23T11:23:44Z | 4b51e14960fd |
| S2 | eCFR, § 860.240 | 21 CFR 860.240, "Procedures for review of a De Novo request"; source note "[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]" | https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-860/subpart-D/section-860.240 | 2026-11-23T11:23:44Z | daf6b3452635 |
| S3 | eCFR, Part 860 (consolidated) | 21 CFR Part 860, "Medical Device Classification Procedures," incl. §§ 860.250, 860.260 | https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-860 | 2026-11-23T11:23:44Z | fffe7e6cc6c5 |
| S4 | GovInfo, CFR annual edition, Subpart D | 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D, CFR 2025 annual edition, edition date 2025-04-01 | https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-part860-subpartD.xml | 2026-11-23T11:23:43Z | ad778f6b1871 |
| S5 | GovInfo, CFR annual edition, § 860.240 | 21 CFR 860.240, CFR 2025 annual edition, edition date 2025-04-01 | https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec860-240.xml | 2026-11-23T11:23:43Z | 0da0c3734ee9 |

Statutory authority referenced but not quoted in this pass: section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C. 360c(f)(2), which is the authority under which Part 860 Subpart D was issued and which § 860.230(c)(3) and § 860.240(a) cite. The two limits asked about are stated directly in the regulatory text at S1 and S2, so the answer does not depend on the statutory wording.

---

## 9. Verification items for the reviewing clinician

| ID | Item | Why it matters | Suggested check |
|---|---|---|---|
| V-1 | Exact statutory text of FD&C Act § 513(f)(2) (21 U.S.C. 360c(f)(2)), including any statutory period and any provision for extending it | § 860.240(a)'s 120 days may track a statutory deadline; a statutory extension clause, if it exists, could modify the practical outside limit | Read § 513(f)(2) in the current U.S. Code; not fetched in this pass |
| V-2 | Full Federal Register amendatory history of Part 860 Subpart D between 2025-04-01 and 2026-11-21 | The version determination in Section 4 rests on the eCFR source note plus a two-text comparison, not on a complete FR sweep | Search FR for "De Novo" / Part 860 amendments in the window |
| V-3 | Whether any Part 860 or FD&C Act provision tolls the 120-day period for additional information submitted during substantive review | Section 5 states no tolling provision appears in the quoted text; a provision elsewhere would change the practical deadline | Read Part 860 Subpart D in full plus § 513(f)(2) |
| V-4 | Definition of "day" in Part 860 (definitions section) and in 21 CFR 10.3 | Section 2 adopts calendar-day counting from the unqualified word "days"; a contrary definition would change every date in Section 6 | Read the definitions sections; not fetched in this pass |
| V-5 | Section number attribution for the quoted paragraphs beginning "(2) The requester fails to provide a complete response ... within 180 days" | The fetched fragment begins mid-section; it is attributed here to § 860.250 (withdrawal) on the basis of surrounding text | Confirm against the printed § 860.250 in S3/S4 |

---

## 10. Bottom line for the reviewer

For a De Novo request received by FDA and accepted without any additional-information submission, under 21 CFR Part 860 as in force on 2026-11-21: FDA must notify the requester whether the request is accepted **within 15 days** of receipt (§ 860.230(a)), and must review the request and send an order granting or declining it **within 120 days** of receipt (§ 860.240(a)). Both periods are counted in calendar days from the date of FDA's receipt of the request, which is also the date of acceptance under § 860.230(b). Because no additional-information submission follows a refusal to accept, the § 860.230(c)(3) re-anchoring does not apply and the 120 days are not restarted.

# DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN / REGULATORY-AFFAIRS REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE, NOT PATIENT CARE, NOT JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC REGULATORY ADVICE

## 0. Question

A sponsor first learns on day 0 that a case qualifies for the ICH E2A seven-day expedited reporting rule. (1) What is the outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies? (2) If that full period is used, what constraint governs the follow-up? (3) By what day, measured from day 0, must the follow-up report that is 'as complete as possible' be provided?

## 1. Answers

| Ask | Answer | Value and unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies of a case qualifying under the E2A seven-day rule is **7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor** (i.e. the clock expires at the end of **day 7**, measured from day 0). | 7 calendar days |
| 2 | Constraint if the full period is used: the **8 calendar days are *additional*** — they run from expiry of the 7-day clock (day 7), **not** from day 0. Using the whole 7 days therefore consumes the entire initial-notification window, and the complete report is due at the end of the eighth day *after* day 7. The follow-up is not due on day 8. | 8 additional calendar days from day 7 |
| 3 | The 'as complete as possible' follow-up report must be provided **by day 15 measured from day 0** (day 0 + 15 calendar days = day 7 + 8 calendar days). | 15 calendar days from day 0 |

Arithmetic check: 7 + 8 = 15. The follow-up date (day 15) is later than the initial outer limit (day 7) by exactly the 8 additional calendar days stated in the guideline; no figure in this answer exceeds or contradicts another.

## 2. Governing text (version named, quoted verbatim)

**Source A — ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline E2A, *Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting*, Step 4 (1994; reproduced as FDA/HHS guidance and as Health Canada *Guidance for Industry ICH Topic E2A*, 1995).** Retrieved copies: https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E2A-Clinical-Safety-Data-Management--Definitions-and-Standards-for-Expedited-Reporting.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T11:27:25Z, sha256 2242c6e208d5) and https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/hc-sc/migration/hc-sc/dhp-mps/alt_formats/hpfb-dgpsa/pdf/prodpharma/e2a-eng.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T11:27:24Z, sha256 8a40c5acf80b).

Section III.A.1 (FDA/HHS copy):

> 'Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report must include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products.'

The Health Canada copy of the same section reads identically except for 'This report **should** include…' in place of 'must'. Note the channel is illustrative ('e.g.'), not prescriptive.

Section III.A.2 (contrast — **not** the rule that applies to this case):

> 'All Other Serious, Unexpected ADRs — Serious, unexpected reactions (ADRs) that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting.'

Section III.A.3 (why an incomplete initial notification is permissible):

> 'Information for final description and evaluation of a case report may not be available within the required time frames for reporting outlined above. Nevertheless, for regulatory purposes, initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met: an identifiable patient; a suspect medicinal product; an identifiable reporting source; and an event or outcome that can be identified as serious and [unexpected] …' (the retrieved excerpt is truncated at 'serious and').

**Source B — ICH E2D(R1), *Post-Approval Safety Data: Definitions and Standards for Management and Reporting of Individual Case Safety Reports*, Section 5.2 'Reporting timeframes'** (used here only to corroborate the day-zero anchor; it does not supply the 7-day rule). Two retrieved copies of the same §5.2 text: ICH database Step 3 draft dated 5 February 2024, https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/ICH_E2D(R1)_Step3_Draft%20Guideline_2024_0205.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T11:27:25Z, sha256 c80617927665); and EMA-hosted PDF whose filename carries 'step-5', https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-e2dr1-guideline-post-approval-safety-data-definitions-standards-management-reporting-individual-case-safety-reports-step-5_en.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T11:27:25Z, sha256 a545b36d045e). The version status of E2D(R1) should be confirmed against the ICH site before citation in a submission; the two retrieved copies agree on the operative sentence:

> 'The regulatory reporting time clock is considered to start on the date when any personnel of the MAH (including third parties, such as service providers and other contractual partners, acting on behalf of the MAH) obtains sufficient information to determine that a case report fulfils the minimum criteria for reporting … This date should be considered day zero unless otherwise specified by regional or local requirements.'

and on restarting:

> 'When additional medically relevant information is received for a previously reported case, the reporting time clock is considered to begin again for submission of the follow-up report, as such day zero for follow-up information is the date the MAH receives the additional information.'

## 3. Population to which the seven-day rule applies

Single cases of serious, unexpected adverse drug reactions (ADRs) that are **fatal or life-threatening**, per E2A Section III.A.1 read with III.A.2 ('All Other Serious, Unexpected ADRs … not fatal or life-threatening' carry the 15-calendar-day deadline). Exposure: the suspect medicinal product, in the dose and route recorded in the case report — E2A does not condition the clock on dose, so the clock is anchored on receipt of qualifying information, not on exposure level. If the case is serious and unexpected but **not** fatal or life-threatening, the correct deadline is 15 calendar days under III.A.2 and no 7-day alert is required; the day-15 figure in Ask 3 above is reached by a different route (7 + 8) and must not be confused with III.A.2. The two rules are textually distinct even though both land on day 15.

## 4. Day 0 and the counting convention

- **Day 0** = the calendar date on which any personnel of the sponsor (including third parties acting on the sponsor's behalf) first received sufficient information to determine that the case meets the minimum reporting criteria (E2A III.A.1 'first knowledge by the sponsor'; E2D(R1) §5.2 'any personnel of the MAH … This date should be considered day zero'). E2A does not use the literal phrase 'day 0'; the anchor is 'first knowledge by the sponsor'. Where a local requirement defines day 0 differently, the local definition governs and this draft must be re-run.
- **Unit: calendar days**, not business days. E2A says 'calendar days' in both the 7-day and the 8-additional-day clauses. Weekends and public holidays do not extend the deadline; a deadline falling on a non-working day must be planned for, not deferred.
- **Counting convention**: 'no later than N calendar days after' a date means the period expires at the end of day 0 + N calendar days. Day 1 is the first calendar day after day 0.
  - Initial notification: expires end of **day 0 + 7**.
  - Complete follow-up: 8 additional days after day 7, i.e. end of **day 0 + 7 + 8 = day 0 + 15**.
- Record the day-0 date (and, for internal audit, the receipt timestamp and time zone) on the case file; the same sponsor case identification number must appear on the initial and the follow-up report (E2A Section V, 'Administrative and Sponsor/Company Details': 'Sponsor/manufacturer's identification number for the case (This number should be the same for the initial and follow-up reports on the same case)').

## 5. Worked example (dates, not times)

Day 0 = Monday 3 March 2025 (date first knowledge by sponsor personnel).

| Milestone | Calendar date | Day number from day 0 |
|---|---|---|
| Day 0 — first knowledge; clock starts | Mon 3 Mar 2025 | 0 |
| Outer limit for initial notification to regulatory agencies (7 calendar days) | Mon 10 Mar 2025 | 7 |
| Complete follow-up report (8 additional calendar days after day 7) | Tue 18 Mar 2025 | 15 |

Check: 10 Mar + 8 days = 18 Mar; 3 Mar + 15 days = 18 Mar. Consistent.

## 6. What each submission must contain

**Initial notification (due by day 7).** May be by telephone, facsimile or in writing (E2A III.A.1). Sufficient to meet the minimum criteria (E2A III.A.3): identifiable patient; suspect medicinal product; identifiable reporting source; an event or outcome identifiable as serious and unexpected. E2A III.A.3 expressly permits the initial report to be submitted within the prescribed time on these minimum criteria even when final description and evaluation are unavailable.

**Complete follow-up (due by day 15).** 'As complete a report as possible', and per E2A III.A.1 it 'must include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products.' Populate the E2A Section V data elements, including: source of report (spontaneous / clinical investigation / literature / other); date the event report was first received by the sponsor; country of occurrence; type of report filed (initial or follow-up — first, second, etc.); sponsor name and address; contact person with telephone and fax; regulatory code or number for the marketing-authorisation dossier or clinical investigation (e.g. IND or CTX number, NDA number); and the case identification number shared with the initial report.

**Later information.** If medically relevant information arrives after the day-15 report, a new clock starts on the date that information is received (E2D(R1) §5.2), producing a further follow-up with its own day 0. A correction issued on internal quality review with no new information does not start a new clock (E2D(R1) §5.2).

## 7. Divergences to verify before this answer is used in any specific jurisdiction

The 7-calendar-day / 8-additional-calendar-day construction above is the ICH E2A text. National implementations may shorten the period, re-define day 0, or prescribe a mandatory format and channel (e.g. a national portal or a specific electronic ICSR standard). The following instruments are the ones to obtain and read in their current version before filing; **their content is not asserted in this draft**, because no verified text for them was available to this analysis:

- European Union: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 520/2012 and GVP Module VI on management and reporting of adverse reactions; the EU ICSR gateway and EudraVigilance submission rules.
- United States: 21 CFR 312.32 (IND safety reports) for investigational drugs; 21 CFR 314.80 (postmarketing reporting) for marketed drugs; FDA guidance on safety reporting for INDs.
- Canada: Food and Drug Regulations C.01.016–C.01.017 and the Health Canada guidance reproduced above.
- Japan: PMDA/MHLW reporting requirements for investigational and post-marketing cases.

Any of these may impose a shorter clock or a different day-counting rule; where they do, the shorter/more specific requirement governs and the day numbers in §1 must be recalculated against that text. Format: E2A does not mandate CIOMS I, MedWatch or a portal; the receiving authority does.

## 8. Statements this draft does not make

It does not assert any national deadline figure, does not assert that any specific case meets the E2A serious/unexpected/fatal-or-life-threatening criteria (that is a clinical causality-and-criteria judgement for the reviewing clinician), and does not address non-expedited reporting or aggregate reporting. It is a draft for qualified review.

IND SERIAL NUMBER DETERMINATION — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED REGULATORY/CLINICAL REVIEW (not medical advice; not for patient care)

1. ANSWER
The next submission to this IND must carry the three-digit serial number 018 (zero-padded; not '18').

2. GOVERNING RULE
21 CFR § 312.23(a)(5) (eCFR, current text as of the date of this review): each submission to an IND is assigned a consecutive three-digit serial number by the sponsor; the original IND is serial 000 and each subsequent submission increments the serial by one (001, 002, 003, ...). Serial numbers are maintained per IND — a sponsor holding more than one IND keeps a separate sequence for each — and the number is assigned by the sponsor, not by FDA (FDA's IND number, e.g. 123456, is a different identifier from the three-digit submission serial).
Citation-verification note: the request refers to 'the supplied eCFR text', but no eCFR text was attached to this request. The paragraph designation (§ 312.23(a)(5)) should be confirmed against the eCFR version on file. The operative rule relied on here — 000 for the original, three digits, +1 for each subsequent submission — is unchanged by that confirmation, and the answer below depends only on the request's premise that all 18 prior submissions were numbered correctly.

3. COUNT OF PRIOR SUBMISSIONS
- Original IND: serial 000 — 1 submission.
- Later submissions: serials 001 through 017 — 17 submissions (017 − 001 + 1 = 17).
- Total prior submissions = 1 + 17 = 18.
- Highest serial number already used = 017.

4. ARITHMETIC (shown so the reviewer can verify)
- Next serial = 000 + 18 = 018.
- Cross-check: highest used serial 017 + 1 = 018. Both routes agree.
- Format check: three digits required, so 018 (018 ≤ 999, within the three-digit field).

5. SERIAL ASSIGNMENT TABLE
| Submission | Serial |
| Original IND | 000 |
| 1st later submission | 001 |
| ... (consecutive) | ... |
| 17th later submission | 017 |
| NEXT submission (the one in question) | 018 |

6. POINTS THE REVIEWER SHOULD CONFIRM AGAINST THE SPONSOR'S IND FILE (none changes the answer if the request's premise holds)
- The original IND was in fact assigned 000 (the conventional starting serial).

REGULATORY DETERMINATION — PREMARKET NOTIFICATION (510(k)) STATUS OF A DEVICE WITHIN THE MEANING OF SECTION 520(b) OF THE FD&C ACT UNDER 21 CFR PART 807, SUBPART E AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21

Prepared by: Regulatory Specialist. This is a regulatory-analysis draft for a qualified regulatory/clinical reviewer; it is not medical advice and is not for patient care.

──────────────────────────────────────────
1. QUESTION PRESENTED
──────────────────────────────────────────
A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

──────────────────────────────────────────
2. DETERMINATION
──────────────────────────────────────────
No. 21 CFR 807.85(a), which sits inside Subpart E and is titled "Exemption from premarket notification," provides: "A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act." Because the question's premise is that the device is within the meaning of section 520(b), the § 807.81(a) obligation does not attach, and the 90-day pre-distribution timing rule in § 807.81(a) has nothing to operate on. There is no premarket notification submission under Subpart E and therefore no 90-day deadline to satisfy before commercial distribution.

Two qualifications govern this answer and must travel with it:

(a) The exemption is conditional. § 807.85(a) exempts only a device "within the meaning of section 520(b)." If any one of the statutory criteria in § 520(b)(1)(A)–(D) fails, the device is not a custom device, § 807.85(a) does not apply, and § 807.81(a) requires a premarket notification submitted to FDA at least 90 days before the manufacturer proposes to begin introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

(b) Exemption from premarket notification is not exemption from all regulation. § 807.85(a) removes only "premarket notification requirements of this subpart." The annual report under section 520(b)(2), establishment registration and device listing (21 CFR Part 807, Subpart B), medical device reporting (21 CFR Part 803) and quality system requirements (21 CFR Part 820) are outside the scope of § 807.85(a) and must be assessed and satisfied separately.

──────────────────────────────────────────
3. SOURCES AND VERSIONS RELIED ON
──────────────────────────────────────────
3.1 21 CFR 807.81 ("When a premarket notification submission is required"). Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 807, Subpart E; page retrieved 2026-11-23T11:32:08Z, sha256 cffa5dd519c4. Source note on the section: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024]." Corroborated against GovInfo, CFR-2025-title21-vol8, Part 807 Subpart E (PDF and XML), retrieved 2026-11-23T11:32:08Z, sha256 c66ba7f9d7af and e0a4b2568d23.

3.2 21 CFR 807.85 ("Exemption from premarket notification"). Same Part 807, Subpart E; eCFR page retrieved 2026-11-23T11:32:08Z, sha256 c74dcd356a8a; GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol8 Part 807 Subpart E PDF, sha256 c66ba7f9d7af; XML, sha256 e0a4b2568d23. Source note: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]."

3.3 FD&C Act § 520(b), 21 U.S.C. 360j(b), as amended by the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act (FDASIA), Pub. L. 112-144, § 617 (July 9, 2012), 126 Stat. 993. Statutory criteria summarised at § 4.5 below.

3.4 Food and Drug Administration, "Custom Device Exemption: Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff" (September 2014), https://www.fda.gov/media/89897/download — as identified and characterised in the Federal Register notice cited at 3.5. (The guidance document itself was not retrieved for this determination; it is cited here only to the extent the Federal Register notice describes it.)

3.5 Federal Register document 2026-14707 (July 22, 2026), Docket No. FDA-2026-N-1849 (notice of a proposed information collection submitted to OMB under the Paperwork Reduction Act), retrieved 2026-11-23T11:32:08Z, sha256 6740b5e614b0. This notice states: "Regulations in 21 CFR 812.3 define a custom device and implementing regulations in 21 CFR 807.85 provide for exemption from premarket notification. Section 520(b) of the FD&C Act also provides for the issuance of guidance. The guidance document entitled, 'Custom Device Exemption' (September 2014) ... explains how FDA interprets provisions in section 520(b)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, describes what information should be submitted in a Custom Device Annual Report ('annual report'), and provides recommendations on how to submit an annual report for devices distributed under the custom device exemption."

──────────────────────────────────────────
4. ANALYSIS
──────────────────────────────────────────
4.1 The baseline rule (§ 807.81(a)). Verbatim: "Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria: (1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II. (2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section. (3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use ..." The 90-day figure is a minimum interval measured in calendar days between submission and the proposed start of commercial distribution; it is not a waiting period that runs after a decision.

4.2 The paragraph (b) carve-outs are not the route to the answer here. § 807.81(b)(1) removes the § 807.81(a) obligation where a premarket approval application under section 515 (or a section 513(f)(2) reclassification petition) is pending, or where there is a cleared predetermined change control plan under section 515C and the change is consistent with it. Neither describes a device that meets section 520(b).

4.3 The operative provision is § 807.85(a). Verbatim: "A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act." The section is located in Subpart E itself; its stated condition is solely the statutory meaning of section 520(b). No unit count, no distribution-volume threshold and no timing condition appear in the text of § 807.85(a) as quoted above.

4.4 Statutory/regulatory interplay — the point that must be got right. Section 520(b)(1) of the FD&C Act, by its own terms, disapplies only "the requirements of sections 514 and 515" (performance standards and premarket approval). It does not, on its face, disapply section 510(k). The premarket-notification exemption for custom devices is supplied by FDA's regulation at 21 CFR 807.85(a), not by the statute alone. FDA describes the arrangement the same way in the 2026 Federal Register notice quoted at 3.5 ("implementing regulations in 21 CFR 807.85 provide for exemption from premarket notification"). Because the question is framed under Part 807, Subpart E, § 807.85(a) is dispositive: within Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, a device within the meaning of section 520(b) is exempt.

4.5 Conditions precedent (all must hold for § 807.85(a) to apply). Section 520(b)(1) as amended by FDASIA § 617 describes a custom device as a device that:
  (A) necessarily deviates from an otherwise applicable performance standard under section 514 or premarket approval requirement under section 515;
  (B) is not generally available in finished form for purchase or for prescription upon such order;
  (C) is not offered for commercial distribution through labeling or advertising; and
  (D) is intended for use by an individual patient named in the order of a physician or other practitioner licensed by law to administer the device, or is intended to meet the special needs of a physician or other practitioner in the course of professional practice.
The population to which the exemption attaches is therefore the specific patient or the specific practitioner identified in the order, for the specific device type described in that order — not a general commercial population. If criterion (B) or (C) fails, for example because the manufacturer also markets a generally available, catalogued version of the same device, the exemption does not reach that version and § 807.81(a) applies to it with the full 90-day pre-distribution interval.

4.6 Editorial note on the eCFR rendering of § 807.85(a). The retrieved eCFR page shows, immediately after the operative sentence quoted at 4.3, two subparagraphs — "(1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons)." These reproduce the pre-2016 formulation of § 807.85(a) and track the pre-FDASIA statute. The operative condition stated in the sentence itself is the meaning of section 520(b); the residual subparagraphs are consistent with, but narrower than, the amended statutory definition and should not be applied as independent gatekeeping criteria in place of § 520(b)(1)(A)–(D).

4.7 Date-of-law verification for 2026-11-21. § 807.81 was last amended at 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024) and § 807.85 at 81 FR 70340 (Oct. 12, 2016); neither source note records any amendment between those dates and the operative date. The eCFR snapshot was retrieved on 2026-11-23, two days after the operative date, and the GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol8 text is identical in the operative respects. The text quoted in § 4.1 and § 4.3 is therefore the text in force on 2026-11-21.

4.8 Obligations that survive the exemption (scope note). (i) Annual report: section 520(b)(2) requires the manufacturer of a device distributed under the exemption to report annually, and FDA's September 2014 guidance describes the content and submission of the Custom Device Annual Report (per the Federal Register characterisation at 3.5, which cites section 520(b)(2)(B)). (ii) Establishment registration and device listing under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart B, medical device reporting under 21 CFR Part 803, and quality system requirements under 21 CFR Part 820 are not addressed by § 807.85(a) and must be evaluated on their own terms. (iii) The exemption is not transferable to a differently configured or generally marketed device.

──────────────────────────────────────────
5. QUANTITIES AND UNITS (every figure with its unit)
──────────────────────────────────────────
• 90 days — the minimum interval, in calendar days, between submission of a premarket notification and the proposed start of commercial distribution, imposed by 21 CFR 807.81(a) on persons required to register. This interval does not apply to the device described in the question.
• May 28, 1976 — the statutory transition date used in § 807.81(a)(1) to define "first time" commercial distribution (a date, not a duration).
• Amendment dates: March 15, 2024 (89 FR 18792) for § 807.81; October 12, 2016 (81 FR 70340) for § 807.85.
• Annual-report information collection, as stated in Federal Register document 2026-14707 (July 22, 2026), Docket No. FDA-2026-N-1849, line "Annual reporting for custom devices under 520(b) of the FD&C Act": 31 respondents; 1 response per respondent; 31 total annual responses; 40 hours average burden per response; 1,240 total annual hours (31 × 40 = 1,240).
• No dose applies; the exposure metric for the annual report is the number of devices distributed during the preceding year, in units of devices.

──────────────────────────────────────────
6. WHAT THE MANUFACTURER SHOULD HOLD IN THE REGULATORY FILE
──────────────────────────────────────────
6.1 The physician's or practitioner's order identifying the individual patient or stating the special need, retained per device and per patient, sufficient to evidence § 520(b)(1)(D).
6.2 A written § 520(b)(1)(A)–(D) analysis for the device type, signed and dated, evidencing the deviation from the otherwise applicable section 514 standard or section 515 requirement (A), that the device is not generally available in finished form (B), that it is not offered for commercial distribution through labeling or advertising (C), and the order-based or special-needs basis (D).
6.3 The annual report under section 520(b)(2) for each year in which devices are distributed, prepared consistent with FDA's "Custom Device Exemption" guidance (September 2014).
6.4 Records demonstrating compliance with registration and listing, medical device reporting and quality system requirements, which § 807.85(a) does not displace.

# Draft for qualified clinician review — not medical advice, not for the care of any individual patient.

## 1. The question as operationalized

**Subject:** a child aged 4 years (i.e., younger than 5 years of age) who has received bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. No other clinical characteristics were supplied (no immunocompromise, no prior TB test, no known TB exposure, no symptoms); the answer is therefore scoped to that minimal description.

**Question:** On the CDC page *Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis* as available on 2026-11-21, does the stated preference for TB blood tests apply to this child?

**Units and quantities:** No drug dose or exposure magnitude is at issue in this question. Every figure in this document is either an **age in years** (4 years; 5 years of age) or a **date**. The single decision threshold is **5 years of age**.

**Answer in one line:** **No.** The page states the TB blood test preference for people **5 years of age and older** who have received BCG, and separately states that current CDC guidelines recommend the **TB skin test** as the method of testing for children **younger than 5 years of age**. A 4-year-old falls on the skin-test side of that boundary. The page also carries an *unqualified* BCG bullet that conflicts with this; see §4.

---

## 2. Ask 1 — the page relied on, with version control

**Primary source (the page named in the request):**

> Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis.* For Health Care Providers. Content date: **Apr. 17, 2025**. URL: https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; page sha256 `9095c1db7f3e`.

**Version-control caveat, stated plainly:** the request fixes the citation date at **2026-11-21**. The snapshot actually retrieved and quoted here was fetched **2026-11-23T11:37:03Z**, i.e. **2 days after** the citation date, and its own on-page content date is **Apr. 17, 2025**. No separate Wayback Machine or CDC-archive capture dated 2026-11-21 was retrieved for this draft. The quoted wording below is therefore the wording of the page as retrieved on 2026-11-23, on a page whose published content date (Apr. 17, 2025) precedes the citation date. A reviewer who requires a strict 2026-11-21 capture should confirm against an archive snapshot of that date before this citation is finalized; if the archive differs, the verdict should be re-read against the archived text.

**Corroborating CDC pages** (used only to confirm that the wording is not an artifact of one page; they are *not* the page the request names, and they are labelled as secondary throughout):

- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical and Laboratory Diagnosis for Tuberculosis.* https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; sha256 `1e221be4a63e`.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Interferon Gamma Release Assay.* Content date May 9, 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/interferon-gamma-release-assay.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; sha256 `4791076e7908`.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test.* https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; sha256 `4aa43e3065d3`.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Health Care Providers — Children (TB) page. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; sha256 `171f6557d84e`.
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *Tuberculosis (TB) — Children* (public-facing). https://www.cdc.gov/tb/about/children.html. Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:37:04Z; sha256 `de6543e1f048`.

---

## 3. Ask 2 — the verdict, read from the primary page's own words

### 3.1 The age-qualified preference statement (the controlling text for this child)

Verbatim from https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/:

> "The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved these two TB blood tests that are commercially available in the United States:
> QuantiFERON®-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus)
> T-SPOT®.TB test (T-Spot)
> Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. **TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.**"

Two conditions are stated conjunctively: (i) **5 years of age and older**, and (ii) **received BCG**. The child satisfies (ii) and fails (i): 4 years < 5 years. **The stated preference does not apply to this child.**

### 3.2 The page's explicit instruction for children under 5

Verbatim from the same page:

> "TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
> **Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children.** Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance1 on the use of TB blood tests in children."

So for a 4-year-old the page's own default is the **Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST)**, with TB blood testing (interferon-gamma release assay, IGRA) acknowledged as something *some experts use* in younger children and as a matter on which the AAP guidance may be consulted. That is a **recommendation of TST as the method**, not a prohibition of IGRA; and it is explicitly framed as a guideline summary, with clinician discretion preserved.

### 3.3 What the page means by "TB blood tests"

The page defines the term itself, so the assumption that "TB blood tests" = IGRAs is verified against the page rather than imported:

> "**TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])** … measure the immune response in whole blood after it has been mixed with controls and with synthetic peptides that are designed to simulate TB antigens … The tests measure the amount of the IFN-γ response."

### 3.4 What the page does **not** say (scope limits relevant to the verdict)

- The page gives **no product-specific age indication** for QFT-Plus or T-SPOT.TB. It names both products as FDA-approved and commercially available in the United States, and then states the age-qualified preference at the level of the *test category*. It does not reconcile the category-level statement with either product's FDA-approved indication. **The FDA-approved age indications in the two product labels were not retrieved for this draft and are not asserted here** — see §6.
- The page does **not** qualify the under-5 recommendation by the child's reason for testing (exposure investigation vs. screening vs. symptoms). The under-5 statement is unconditional as written. The page does separately say, for interpretation, that if a patient has signs or symptoms of TB disease, providers should not wait for TB blood test or TB skin test results before starting other diagnostic tests — that is a statement about diagnostic work-up urgency, not about which infection test to choose.
- The page **does not** distinguish U.S. from non-U.S. settings for the age boundary; the BCG context is described only as "given to infants and small children in countries where TB is common" and "not generally used in the United States."
- The AAP guidance referenced as footnote 1 on the page **was not retrieved**; the page's pointer to it is quoted, but its content is not summarized here.

---

## 4. The genuine conflict on the page — stated, not smoothed over

The **same primary page** also contains an *unqualified* BCG bullet, in its "Selecting a test" section:

> "Health care providers are encouraged to use TB blood tests to detect TB infection. **TB blood tests are preferred for:
> People who have received the BCG vaccine** and
> People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation.
> TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
> Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age."

Read in isolation, the bolded bullet would reach a 4-year-old with BCG. Read in sequence — as it appears on the page — it is immediately followed by the under-5 TST recommendation, and it is contradicted in terms by the age-qualified statement in §3.1 ("5 years of age and older").

**Why the age-qualified statement controls for this child:** (a) it is the only formulation on the page that specifies *who* the BCG preference covers, and it does so by explicit age threshold; (b) the page states the under-5 TST recommendation twice in substance on the same page (once in the TB blood test section, once in the TB skin test section); (c) the unqualified bullet is a summary list item with no population qualifier and cannot be read as silently deleting the explicit "5 years of age and older" that appears elsewhere on the same page.

**This is an internal inconsistency in the source, and it is material** — a clinician reading only the "Selecting a test" box would form the opposite impression. The verdict of "No" is correct on the page's age-qualified text, but the reviewer should know the page is not internally clean on this point.

### 4.1 The conflict is replicated on CDC's sibling pages (corroboration of the same tension)

- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html: "TB blood tests are preferred for: People who have received the BCG vaccine and People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation." — followed immediately by "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age." (No age qualifier on the BCG bullet; no age qualifier needed on the TST sentence.)
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/interferon-gamma-release-assay.html: "TB blood tests are the preferred method of testing for: People who have received the BCG vaccine …" and, under "Age": "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children … The collection of a sufficient blood sample can be a practical barrier to testing very young children with a TB blood test."
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html: "**BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.**" — note: this sentence says "including children" with **no age floor**, which is the sharpest form of the conflict with the 5-year threshold. The same page, under "Age," again states the under-5 TST recommendation.
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html: "Health care providers should recommend the TB blood test if a child: **Is five years of age or older** and **Has ever received the BCG vaccine** (TB vaccine). Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by the BCG vaccine."
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/about/children.html: "**TB blood tests are the preferred tests for people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG TB vaccine.**" and "If a child is 5 years of age or older and has ever received a vaccine for TB, their health care provider should recommend the TB blood test."

**Net reading of the CDC corpus retrieved:** four of these six pages state the 5-year floor explicitly or state the under-5 TST recommendation; the tuberculin-skin-test page's "including children" sentence and the unqualified BCG bullets are the outliers. For a **4-year-old**, the weight of the retrieved CDC text is that the blood-test preference is **not** stated to apply, and the TST is the stated method.

---

## 5. Boundary table for the reviewing clinician (what changes with age)

| Subject age | BCG history | Does the page's stated TB blood test preference apply? | Page text that decides it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **4 years (this child)** | Yes | **No** — outside the stated preference; TST is the stated method for children younger than 5 years | "preferred … for people 5 years of age and older who have received the … BCG vaccine"; "recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age" |
| Exactly 5 years | Yes | **Yes** — the preference is stated as "5 years of age and older" | same sentence |
| 6 years or older | Yes | **Yes** | same sentence |
| Any age, no BCG, unlikely to return for TST reading | No | **Yes** on the second stated ground ("might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation") — not applicable to this child as described | "TB blood tests are preferred for: … People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation" |

The 4-vs-5 boundary is the whole of the answer. It is a **stated age threshold on the page**, not an inference: the page writes "5 years of age and older" for the preference and "younger than 5 years of age" for the TST recommendation.

---

## 6. Where the evidence is thin, absent, or conflicting — flagged for the reviewer

1. **Archived 2026-11-21 capture not obtained.** The retrieved snapshot is 2026-11-23T11:37:03Z; the page's own content date is Apr. 17, 2025. The citation date is satisfied in substance (the page text predates it) but not by a date-matched archive capture. *Action for the reviewer:* confirm against a 2026-11-21 archive snapshot before the citation is finalized.
2. **Internal conflict in the source** (§4): the unqualified BCG preference bullets, and especially the tuberculin-skin-test page's "preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, **including children**," contradict the 5-year floor. The verdict here rests on the age-qualified text and on the repeated under-5 TST recommendation; the conflict is not resolved by anything in the retrieved pages.
3. **Product labels not retrieved.** The page names QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and T-SPOT.TB as the two FDA-approved tests but gives no per-product age indication. The FDA-approved indications of those two labels (including any minimum-age statement) were **not** retrieved for this draft and are **not** asserted here. If the reviewer needs the label-level position for a 4-year-old, that is a separate retrieval from the approved package inserts, and it should be cited to the specific label and section.
4. **AAP guidance (page footnote 1) not retrieved.** The page tells providers they "may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children." The content of that guidance is not summarized here.
5. **The child's indication for testing is unspecified.** The page's under-5 statement does not vary by indication, so the verdict does not turn on it — but if this child has **signs or symptoms of TB disease**, the page separately directs that providers not wait for TB blood test or TB skin test results before starting other diagnostic tests. That is a clinical-urgency point outside the scope of the preference question and is noted only so it is not lost.
6. **No dose or exposure magnitude is in scope.** BCG receipt is treated as a yes/no history. No dose, volume, or concentration figures are used or implied anywhere in this document; the only units are years (ages) and calendar dates.

## 7. Bottom line for the reviewing clinician

question: Y168
answer:
REGULATORY MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW
Subject: Whether 'the research is minimal risk' is by itself a sufficient basis to enroll a subject in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation without informed consent under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21; and the Part 50 definition of 'minimal risk'.
Status: Draft for review by a qualified clinician and the reviewing IRB. Not legal advice. Not for the care of any individual subject. No protocol-specific facts are assumed.

=====================================================================
1. QUESTIONS AND SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

Q1 (verdict). An investigator says an FDA-regulated clinical investigation may enroll a person without informed consent solely because the research is minimal risk. Under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21, is that reason sufficient?

A1. NO. Minimal risk is necessary but not sufficient. Since the codification of 21 CFR 50.22 ('Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations'), no more than minimal risk is criterion (a) of five findings that the IRB — not the investigator — must make and document before an IRB may approve a consent procedure that omits or alters any element of § 50.25(a) or (b), or waive consent entirely. An investigator's own conclusion that a study is minimal risk has no operative legal effect and, standing alone, does not authorize enrollment without consent. Separately, in the two emergency pathways (§ 50.23 and § 50.24) minimal risk is not the operative test at all.

Q2 (value). How does Part 50 define 'minimal risk'?

A2. 21 CFR 50.3(k). Verbatim: 'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

=====================================================================

Nothing in the retrieved text suggests any such change.

=====================================================================
3. ANSWER TO Q1 IN FULL — WHY 'MINIMAL RISK' ALONE IS NOT SUFFICIENT
=====================================================================

3.1 The operative provision: 21 CFR 50.22

Section 50.22, as verified in S1, reads in full:

'§ 50.22 Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations.
The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation described in this section may approve an informed consent procedure that does not include or that alters some or all of the elements of informed consent set forth in § 50.25(a) and (b), or may waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following:
(a) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;
(b) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;
(c) If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format;
(d) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and
(e) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.'

3.2 The five findings, and the role minimal risk plays

| Criterion | What must be found | Who finds it | Independent of minimal risk? |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | The investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects | IRB | This is the minimal-risk element |
| (b) | The investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration | IRB | Yes — a separate, fact-specific practicality judgment |
| (c) | If identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are used, the investigation could not practicably be carried out without using them in identifiable form | IRB | Yes — triggered only where identifiable information/biospecimens are involved |
| (d) | The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects | IRB | Yes |
| (e) | Whenever appropriate, subjects or legally authorized representatives receive additional pertinent information after participation | IRB | Yes — post-participation debriefing |

The structure of the sentence is conjunctive: the IRB 'may ... waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following: (a) ... (b) ... (c) ... (d) ... and (e).' All five must be satisfied and documented. A finding of no more than minimal risk discharges (a) only.

3.3 Three independent reasons the investigator's stated reason fails as stated

(i) It answers only one of five criteria. Even a correct minimal-risk determination leaves (b), (c), (d) and (e) unaddressed. Criterion (b) in particular is not implied by low risk: a minimal-risk study that could practicably be carried out with consent (e.g., a survey, a single extra blood draw at a scheduled visit, a review of records where consent is feasible) does not satisfy (b) merely because it is low risk. Low risk and impracticability are different questions.

(ii) The finding belongs to the IRB, not the investigator. Section 50.22 confers the authority on 'the IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation'. The investigator's own classification of the study as minimal risk is not a legal authorization to enroll anyone without consent. Enrolling on that basis is a departure from the consent requirements of §§ 50.25 and 50.27 and from the IRB-approved protocol.

(iii) The findings must be documented. Section 50.22 requires the IRB to 'find and document'. A verbal or assumed understanding is not sufficient; the investigator should hold a written IRB determination (typically the approval letter and minutes) recording each of (a)-(e) before the first enrollment without consent.

3.4 What minimal risk does and does not do

- It does: make a study eligible for IRB consideration of waiver or alteration of consent under § 50.22, alongside the other four findings.
- It does not: waive consent by operation of law; transfer the decision to the investigator; dispense with any of (b)-(e); or apply at all to the emergency pathways in §§ 50.23 and 50.24.
- Historical note: before § 50.22 was codified, FDA's Part 50 contained no general IRB authority to waive consent for minimal-risk research; the only consent exceptions were the emergency provisions (§§ 50.23 and 50.24) and the separate waiver of documentation at § 56.109(c). Under that earlier state of the regulation the investigator's statement would have been wrong outright. It is now wrong in part — the premise is a permissible predicate but not a sufficient one. Confirm the § 50.22 effective date against the Federal Register (S6) before relying on this history externally.

3.5 The other consent pathways — minimal risk is not the test

(a) 21 CFR 50.23 — emergency use of a test article in an individual patient. Per S2, even in an emergency the investigator must obtain consent unless both the investigator and a physician not otherwise participating in the investigation certify in writing all four of the following [21 CFR 50.23(a)]:
  1. The subject is confronted by a life-threatening situation necessitating the use of the test article.
  2. Informed consent cannot be obtained because of an inability to communicate with, or obtain legally effective consent from, the subject.
  3. Time is not sufficient to obtain consent from the subject's legally authorized representative.
  4. No alternative method of approved or generally recognized therapy is available that provides an equal or greater likelihood of saving the subject's life.
  None of these four conditions is 'minimal risk'. A minimal-risk study cannot use § 50.23, and § 50.23 does not require or permit a minimal-risk justification.

(b) 21 CFR 50.24 — planned emergency research. Per S2 and S3, § 50.24 covers planned research in life-threatening emergent situations in which prospective informed consent is waived; the research must hold out the prospect of direct benefit to the subjects, the research plan must be approved in advance by FDA and the IRB, and additional protections must be included (e.g., consultation with and public disclosure to the communities in which the research will be conducted or from which subjects will be drawn, or both). Per S7 and S8, the IRB applies the § 50.24 criteria and FDA's guidance flow-chart (Appendix C), a data monitoring committee provides oversight, and consent is sought as soon as reasonably possible from the legally authorized representative or the subject on regain of capacity. This pathway is directed at research that holds out direct benefit in a life-threatening setting — the opposite end of the risk spectrum from minimal risk — and minimal risk is not one of its criteria.

(c) 21 CFR 50.23(d) — the Department of Defense / Presidential waiver mechanism. Per S1, this provision operates through a set of DOD-specific standards and certifications (including FDA concluding the IND may proceed subject to a Presidential decision, DOD training of personnel and potential recipients, a justified time period not to exceed one year unless separately renewed, a continuing reporting obligation to FDA and the President, and public notice in the Federal Register). It is unavailable to an ordinary sponsor-investigator and does not turn on minimal risk.

3.6 The most likely source of the investigator's confusion: 21 CFR 56.109(c)

A separate provision, 21 CFR 56.109(c) (S5 — cited from codified text, to be re-verified), permits an IRB to waive the requirement for the investigator to obtain a SIGNED consent form — i.e., to waive DOCUMENTATION of consent, not consent itself — where either (1) the only record linking the subject and the research would be the consent document and the principal risk would be potential harm from a breach of confidentiality, or (2) the research presents no more than minimal risk of harm to subjects and involves no procedures for which written consent is normally required outside the research context. Criterion (2) is the one place in the FDA regulations where minimal risk carries most of the weight — but it still requires the second clause (no procedures for which written consent is normally required outside the research context), and it waives only the signature. The subject is still consented, ordinarily orally, and the consent is still documented in the case record. If the investigator's real problem is that a signature is burdensome rather than that consent itself is impossible, § 56.109(c) is the correct provision, not § 50.22.

3.7 Decision procedure the study team should apply

Step 1. Confirm the investigation is FDA-regulated and within the scope of Part 50 (21 CFR 50.1) and Part 56 (21 CFR 56.101). If it is regulated only by the Common Rule (45 CFR 46), this memo does not control; note that 45 CFR 46.116(f) contains parallel waiver criteria.
Step 2. Is this a life-threatening emergency in an individual patient? → § 50.23, with the four written certifications. Is this planned emergency research in a life-threatening condition holding out direct benefit? → § 50.24, with advance FDA and IRB approval, community consultation, public disclosure and data monitoring. Minimal risk is not the test in either.
Step 3. Otherwise, if the study is no more than minimal risk AND could not practicably be carried out with consent AND (where identifiable private information or biospecimens are used) could not practicably be carried out in de-identified form AND the waiver will not adversely affect rights and welfare AND post-participation information will be provided where appropriate → submit for IRB findings under § 50.22. Do not enroll until the written determination is in hand.
Step 4. If consent will be obtained but a signature is the problem → § 56.109(c) documentation waiver.
Step 5. If none of the above → full compliance with §§ 50.25 (elements) and 50.27 (documentation).

=====================================================================
4. ANSWER TO Q2 IN FULL — HOW PART 50 DEFINES MINIMAL RISK
=====================================================================

4.1 The definition (21 CFR 50.3(k))

'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

4.2 Element-by-element reading

| Element | Text | What it requires |
|---|---|---|
| Two dimensions | 'probability and magnitude' | Both the likelihood and the severity of the anticipated harm or discomfort are assessed together; neither alone is decisive |
| Scope of outcome | 'harm or discomfort' | Covers discomfort (e.g., pain, nausea, anxiety, embarrassment), not only physical injury |
| Timing and basis | 'anticipated in the research' | A prospective judgment about the research procedures as proposed, made at review |
| Attribution | 'in and of themselves' | The research procedures are judged on their own risk, not netted against anticipated benefit and not diluted by the risk of the subject's underlying condition |
| Comparator | 'not greater ... than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests' | A relative, not absolute, standard; the two comparators are stated in the alternative |

4.3 What the definition does not do — three points a reviewer must not assume

(i) There is no numeric threshold. Part 50 attaches no percentage, no probability bound, no severity grade and no absolute risk figure to 'minimal risk'. Any protocol or IRB worksheet that assigns a number to the threshold is applying local policy, not the regulatory text.

(ii) Part 50 does not state whose 'daily life' is the comparator. The text says 'those ordinarily encountered in daily life', without specifying whether the reference is the general adult population or the population actually being enrolled (for whom daily life may already involve frequent procedures). This is unresolved on the face of § 50.3(k). The IRB should state explicitly in its minutes which comparator it applied, so the determination is reviewable.

(iii) Minimal risk is a threshold, not a benefit finding. Meeting it says nothing about whether the research is worthwhile, whether risks are minimized under 21 CFR 56.111(a)(1), or whether the risk/benefit relationship is acceptable under 21 CFR 56.111(a)(2). Those are separate IRB findings.

4.4 Where the term is used in Part 50 (verified in S1 unless noted)

- § 50.22(a): 'no more than minimal risk to the subjects' — the waiver/alteration threshold discussed in section 3.
- § 50.51: clinical investigations involving no greater than minimal risk to children — the IRB must find no greater than minimal risk and adequate provisions for assent and parental permission (§ 50.55).
- § 50.52: investigations involving more than minimal risk to children but presenting the prospect of direct benefit — the IRB must find the risk is justified by the anticipated benefit.
- §§ 50.53 and 50.54 (S4, not in fetched set — re-verify): the remaining pediatric risk categories, which are also defined by reference to the same minimal-risk line.

In every one of these uses the term functions the same way: as a threshold that triggers a specific set of additional IRB findings, never as a stand-alone authorization.
